¶
'''withsayer†''' (wiᴛ̵ʜ-sā′ėr), ''n.'' [ME. ''withseier''; ''withsay'' + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] One who withsays; an opponent.

{{smaller block|That he be myȝti to much styre in holsum doctryne, and the ''withseieris'' to with stonde.
{{right|''Wyclif'', Pref. Ep., p. 63.}}}}

'''withset†''' (wiᴛ̵ʜ-set′), ''v. t.'' [< ME. ''withsetten'' (= G. ''widersetzen''); < ''with''<sup>1</sup> + ''set''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.''] To set against; resist; oppose; withstand.

{{smaller block|<poem>More-ouer thou hast holi writt
that cleerli schewith thee goostli liȝt
How thou schuldist deedli synne ''with-sett.''</poem>
{{right|''Political Poems'', etc. (ed. Furnivall), p. 185.}}
<poem>Of God the more grace thou hast serteyn,
If thou ''with-sett'' the devyl in his dede.</poem>
{{right|''Coventry Mysteries'', p. 212.}}}}

'''with-sit†''', ''v. t.'' [ME. ''withsitten''; < ''with'' + ''sit''<sup>1</sup>.] To oppose; contradict; withstand.

{{smaller block|<poem>Was no beggere so bolde bote-yf he blynde were,
That dorst ''with-sitte'' that Peeres seyde for fere of syre
Hunger.</poem>
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (C), ix. 202.}}}}

'''withstand''' (wiᴛ̵ʜ-stand′), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''withstood'', ppr. ''withstanding''. [< ME. ''withstanden'', ''withstonden'' (pret. ''withstod'', pp. ''withstonde''), < AS. ''withstandan'' (pret. ''withstōd'', pp. ''withstanden'') (= Icel. ''vithstanda''; cf. G. ''widerstehen''), resist, withstand, < ''with'', against, + ''standan'', stand: see ''with''<sup>1</sup> and ''stand'', ''v.''] '''I.''' ''trans.'' To stand against; oppose; resist, either with physical or with moral force: frequently with an implication of effectual resistance; resist or oppose successfully: as, to ''withstand'' the storm.

{{smaller block|<poem>My goynge graunted is by parlament
So ferforth that it may not be ''withstonde.''</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, iv. 1298.}}}}
readings.c3s3:
{{smaller block|''Wythstande'' the seruaunte that praysith the, for ellys he thynkyth the for to deceyve.
{{right|''Political Poems'', etc. (ed. Furnivall), p. 31.}}}}

{{smaller block|When Peter was come to Antioch, I ''withstood'' him to the face.
{{right|Gal. ii. 11.}}}}

{{smaller block|Youth and health have ''withstood'' well the involuntary and voluntary hardships of her lot.
{{right|''George Eliot'', Mill on the Floss, v. 1.}}}}

{{smaller block|<poem>Poor beauty! Time and fortune’s wrong
No shape nor feature may ''withstand;''
The wrecks are scattered all along,
Like emptied sea-shells on the sand.</poem>
{{right|''O. W. Holmes'', Mare Rubrum.}}}}
='''Syn.''' ''Resist'', etc. (see ''oppose''), confront, face.

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To make a stand; resist; show resistance.
{{smaller block|<poem>All affermyt hit fast with a fyn wyll,
Saue Ector the honerable, that egerly ''with-stod'',
Disasent to the dede, & dernely he sayde
“Hit is falshed in faythe & of fer cast!”</poem>
{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 7849.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>But Fate ''withstands'', and to oppose the attempt
Medusa with Gorgonian terrour guards
The ford.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., ii. 610.}}}}

'''withstander''' (wiᴛʜ-stan′dėr), ''n.'' [< ''withstand'' + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] One who withstands; an opponent; a resisting power.

'''withwind''' (with′wīnd), ''n.'' [Also ''withywind;'' < ME. ''withwinde'', ''withewynde'', < AS. ''withewinde'', ''withwinde'' (= MD. ''wedewinde;'' cf. Icel. ''vithvindill'' = Dan. ''vedbende''), < ''withthe'', ''withig'', a flexible twig, + *''winde'', < ''windan'', wind: see ''withe'', ''withy'', and ''wind''<sup>1</sup>.] The bindweed, ''Convolvulus''

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|within|6955|withwind}}</noinclude>{{nop}}{{smaller block|The grete and olde cytie of Anthyoche, where seynt Petre preched and dyd many myracles, and there he baptysed aboue .x.M. men ''within'' .vij. dayes.
{{right|''Sir R. Guylforde'', Pylgrymage, p. 48.}}}}
{{smaller block|We arrived ''within'' this hour.
{{right|''Sheridan'', The Rivals, i. 2.}}}}
(''c''†) Not exceeding the space of; during; throughout.
{{smaller block|He should maintaine possession in some of those vast Countries ''within'' the tearme of sixe years.
{{right|''Capt. John Smith'', Works, I. 80.}}}}
(''d'') So as not to exceed or overpass; under; below: as, to live ''within'' one’s income.
{{smaller block|Alle the children that weren in Bethlem, and in alle the eendis of it, fro two ȝeer age and ''with ynne.''
{{right|''Wyclif'', Mat. ii. 16.}}}}
{{smaller block|’Tis a good rule, eat ''within'' your Stomack, act ''within'' your Commission.
{{right|''Selden'', Table-Talk, p. 88.}}}}
{{smaller block|I therefore bid them look upon themselves as no better than a kind of assassins and murderers ''within'' the law.
{{right|''Addison'', Tatler, No. 131.}}}}
'''5.''' In; in the purview, scope, or sphere of action of.
{{smaller block|<poem>Againe I see, ''within'' my glass of Steele,
But foure estates, to serue eche country Soyle.</poem>
{{right|''Gascoigne'', Steele Glas (ed. Arber), p. 57.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Both he and she are still ''within'' my pow’r.</poem>
{{right|''Dryden'', Aurengzebe, i. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|After living for three years ''within'' the subtile influence of an intellect like Emerson’s.
{{right|''Hawthorne'', Scarlet Letter, Int., p. 27.}}}}
'''6†.''' In advance of; before.
{{smaller block|The fifth [time of prayer], two houres ''within'' night, before they goe to sleepe.
{{right|''Purchas'', Pilgrimage, p. 292.}}}}
{{smaller block|It was seen, several nights together, in the west, about an hour ''within'' the night.
{{right|''N. Morton'', New England’s Memorial, p. 325.}}}}
'''7†.''' All but; lacking.

{{smaller block|I served three years, ''within'' a bit, under his honour, in the Royal Inniskillions. {{right|''Sheridan'', St. Patrick’s Day, i. 1.}}}}

{{smaller|'''To get within one†.''' See ''get''<sup>1</sup>.—'''Wheels within wheels.''' See ''wheel''<sup>1</sup>.—'''Within call, compass, hail,''' etc. See the nouns.—'''Within land†''', inland.}}
{{smaller block|The Pories dwell an hundred miles ''within Land'', are low like the Wayanasses, liue on Pinenuts, and small Cocos as bigge as Apples. {{right|''Purchas'', Pilgrimage, p. 840.}}}}
{{smaller|'''Within one’s hand.''' See ''hand''.}}

'''withinforth†''' (wi-ᴛ̵ʜin′fōrth), ''adv.''   [< ME. ''withinne-forth;'' < ''within'' + ''forth''<sup>1</sup>.]   Within.
{{smaller block|The formes that resten ''withinne-forth''. {{right|''Chaucer'', Boëthius, v. prose 5.}}}}
{{smaller block|Beware of the false prophetes that come to you in the clothinge of shepe, and yet ''withinfurth'' been rauenous wolues. {{right|''Sir T. More'', Works, p. 281.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Withinforth'', farther into the firme land, inhabite the Candei. {{right|''Holland'', tr. of Pliny, vi. 29.}}}}

'''withinside''' (wi-ᴛ̵ʜin′sīd), ''adv.''   [< ''within'' + ''side''<sup>1</sup>.]   In the inner part; on the inside.
{{smaller block|A small oval picture of a young lady . . . that was fixed in a pannel ''within-side'' of the door. {{right|''Graves'', Spiritual Quixote, iv. 12.}}}}

'''withnay†''' (wiᴛ̵ʜ-nā′), ''v. t.''   [< ME. ''withnayen;'' < ''with-'' + ''nay''.]   To refuse; deny.
{{smaller block|<poem>Yit if thai ''withnay''
Her fruyt, the fattest roote away thai tere.</poem>{{right|''Palladius'', Husbondrie (E. E. T. S.), p. 102.}}}}

'''without''' (wi-ᴛ̵ʜout′), ''adv.'', ''prep.'', and ''conj.''   [< ME. ''withoute'', ''withouten'', ''withute'', ''withuten'', ''witute'', ''wituten'', < AS. ''withūtan'' (= Icel. ''vithutan''), on the outside of, < ''with'', against, + ''ūtan'', outside, from without: see ''out''.]   '''I.''' ''adv.'' '''1.''' On or as to the outside; outwardly; externally.
{{smaller block|Pitch it [the ark] within and ''without''. {{right|Gen. vi. 14.}}}}
{{smaller block|The Dukes Palace seemeth to be faire, but I was not in it, onely I saw it ''without.'' {{right|''Coryat'', Crudities, I. 99.}}}}
'''2.''' Out of doors; outside, as of a room or a house.
{{smaller block|Sir, there ’s a gentlewoman ''without'' would speak with your worship.
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Knight of Burning Pestle, iv. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Their doors are barr’d against a bitter flout:
Snarl, if you please, but you shall snarl ''without.''</poem>
{{right|''Dryden'', tr. of Persius’s Satires, i. 217.}}}}
'''3.''' As regards external acts or the outer life; externally.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Without'' unspotted, innocent within,
She feared no danger, for she knew no sin.</poem>
{{right|''Dryden'', Hind and Panther, i. 3.}}}}
{{smaller|'''From without''', from the outside: opposed to ''from within:'' as, sounds ''from without'' reached their ears.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>These were ''from without''
The growing miseries. ''Milton'', P. L., x. 714.</poem>}}
{{smaller block|The object of the historian’s imitation is not within him, it is furnished ''from without.''
{{right|''Macaulay'', Sir James Mackintosh.}}}}

'''II.''' ''prep.'' '''1.''' Outside of; at or on the exterior or outside of; external to; out of: opposed to ''within:'' as, ''without'' the walls.
{{smaller block|With in the Cytee and ''with oute'' ben many fayre Gardynes, and of dyverse frutes.
{{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 123.}}}}
{{smaller block|Then ''without'' the doore, thrice to the South, every one bowing his knee in honour of the fire.
{{right|''Capt. John Smith'', Works, I. 34.}}}}
{{smaller block|I do not feel it, I do not think of it; it is a thing ''without'' me.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Bartholomew Fair, iv. 4.}}}}

{{smaller block|Their boat was cast away upon a strand ''without'' Long Island.
{{right|''Winthrop'', Hist. New England, II. 39.}}}}
{{smaller block|At such a time the mind of the prosperous man goes, as it were, abroad, among things ''without'' him.
{{right|''Steele'', Spectator, No. 19.}}}}
{{smaller block|I was received . . . with great civility by the superior, who met us ''without'' the gate.
{{right|''Pococke'', Description of the East, II. i. 225.}}}}

'''2.''' Out of the limits, compass, range, reach, or powers of; beyond.
{{smaller block|<poem>The ages that succeed, and stand far off
To gaze at your high prudence, shall admire,
And reckon it an act ''without'' your sex.</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Sejanus, ii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|As to the Palace of Versailles (which is yet some Miles further, within the Mountainous Country, not unlike Black-Heath or Tunbridge), ’tis ''without'' dispute the most magnificent of any in Europe.
{{right|''Lister'', Journey to Paris, p. 201.}}}}
{{smaller block|Eternity, before the world and after, is ''without'' our reach.
{{right|''T. Burnet'', Theory of the Earth.}}}}

'''3.''' Lacking; destitute of; exempt or free from; unconnected with; independent of: noting loss, absence, negation, privation, etc.: as, to be ''without'' money; to do ''without'' sleep; ''without'' possibility of error; ''without'' harm.
{{smaller block|Thei seyn that, whan he schalle come in to another World, he schalle not ben ''with outen'' an Hows, ne ''with owten'' Hors, ne ''with outen'' Gold and Sylver.
{{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 253.}}}}
{{smaller block|Noe times have bene ''without'' badd men.
{{right|''Spenser'', State of Ireland.}}}}
{{smaller block|Now, ladies, to glad your aspects once again with the sight of Love, and make a spring smile in your faces, which must have looked like winter ''without'' me.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Challenge at Tilt.}}}}

{{smaller block|King John lived to have three Wives. His first was Alice, Daughter of Hubert Earl of Morton, who left him a Widower ''without'' Issue.
{{right|''Baker'', Chronicles, p. 74.}}}}
{{smaller block|Hee gave him wisdome at his request, and riches ''without'' asking.
{{right|''Milton'', Apology for Smectymnuus.}}}}
{{smaller block|Having marked the hour of relieving guard, and made all necessary observations, he retired ''without'' being discovered.
{{right|''Irving'', Granada, p. 29.}}}}
{{smaller block|The darkness was intense, we were ignorant of the ford and ''without'' guides, and were encumbered with nearly two hundred wounded, whom we were unwilling to abandon.
{{right|''The Century'', XLI. 411.}}}}
{{smaller block|In colloquial language the object is frequently omitted after this preposition, especially in such phrases as ''to do without, to go without'': as, they can give me no assistance, so I must ''do without.''
<poem>And nice affections wavering stood in doubt
If best were as it is, or best ''without.''</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Lover’s Complaint, l. 98.}}}}
{{smaller|'''Cold without.''' See ''cold.''—'''Indorsement without recourse.''' See ''indorsement.''—'''To go without saying.''' See ''go.''—'''Without book, day, dispute, distinction, dread†.''' See the nouns.—'''Without fail.''' See ''fail''<sup>1</sup>.—'''Without more bones.''' See ''bone''<sup>1</sup>.—'''Without prejudice, price, reserve.''' See the nouns.}}

'''III.''' ''conj.'' ''Without'' is sometimes used to govern a substantive clause introduced by ''that'', ''without that'' thus signifying unless, except; and then, the ''that'' being omitted, it obtains the value of a conjunction (like ''because, while, since'', etc.) in the same sense; but it is now rarely, if ever, used thus by careful and correct speakers and writers.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Withoute that'' she myght have his loue ageyn,
She were on don for euere in certayne.</poem>
{{right|''Generydes'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 475.}}}}

{{smaller block|And it is so sumptuous and so straunge a werke that it passeth fer my reason and vnderstondynge to make any reporte of it, ''without'' I shulde apayre the fame thereof.
{{right|''Sir R. Guylforde'', Pylgrymage, p. 79.}}}}
{{smaller block|He may stay him; marry, not ''without'' the prince be willing.
{{right|''Shak.'', Much Ado, iii. 3. 86.}}}}
{{smaller block|We should make no mention of what concerns ourselves, ''without'' it be of matters wherein our friends ought to rejoice.
{{right|''Steele'', Spectator, No. 100.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I needs must break
These bonds that so defame me: not ''without''
She wills it: would I if she will’d it?</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Lancelot and Elaine.}}}}

'''without-door''' (wi-ᴛ̵ʜout′dōr), ''a.'' Outdoor; exterior; outward; external.
{{smaller block|Praise her but for this her ''without-door'' form.
{{right|''Shak.'', W. T., ii. 1. 69.}}}}

'''withoute†''', '''withouten†''', ''adv.'', ''prep.'', and ''conj.'' Obsolete forms of ''without.''

'''without-forth†''' (wi-ᴛ̵ʜout′fōrth), ''adv.''   [< ME. ''without forth'', ''with-oute forth'', ''withouten-forth''; < ''without'' + ''forth''<sup>1</sup>.]   Without.
{{smaller block|Ymagynaciouns of sensible things weeren enpreynted into sowles fro bodies ''withoute-forth.''
{{right|''Chaucer'', Boëthius, iv. meter 4.}}}}
{{smaller block|Also rarely used adjectively.}}
{{smaller block|The ''wythoutforth'' [var. ''foreyn'', p. 33] landys and tenementis of citezens which shalbe mynesters of the cite shalbe bounde to conserue theym ageynst the Kynge vndamaged for there offyces as there tenementis wythin the citee.
{{right|''Arnold’s Chron.'' (1502), p. 9.}}}}

'''withoutside†''' (wi-ᴛ̵ʜout′sīd), ''adv.''   [< ''without'' + ''side''<sup>1</sup>.]   Outside; externally; on the outside.

{{smaller block|Not meeting with him, I fancy’d he had some private Way up the Chimney. . . . So, Sir, I turn’d my Coat here, to save it clean, and up I scrambled; but when I came ''withoutside'', I saw nobody there.
{{right|''Mrs. Centlivre'', Marplot, ii. 1.}}}}

{{smaller block|Why does that lawyer wear black? does he carry his conscience ''withoutside?'' {{right|''Congreve'', Love for Love, iv. 6.}}}}

'''withsafe†''' (wiᴛ̵ʜ-sāf′), ''v.''   [Early mod. E. ''wythsafe'', ''witsafe'', ''withsave''; appar. an artificial formation, < ''with-'' + ''safe'', in imitation of ''vouchsafe''. There may have been some confusion with ''withsay'', ''withsay'' implying ‘oppose’ and ''withsafe'' ‘consent.’]   '''I.''' ''trans.'' To make safe; assure.
{{smaller block|<poem>Now must I seek some other ways
Myself for to ''withsave''.</poem>
{{right|''Wyatt'', He Repenteth that He had Ever Loved.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To vouchsafe; deign.
{{smaller block|I ''wythsafe'', I am content to do a thyng. Je daigne. . . . I was wonte to crouche and knele to hym, and I do nat ''withsafe'' to looke upon hym. {{right|''Palsgrave'', p. 783.}}}}

'''withsain†.''' Infinitive of ''withsay''.   ''Chaucer.''

'''withsay†''' (wiᴛ̵ʜ-sā′), ''v. t.''   [ME. ''withseyen'', ''withseggen'', ''withsiggen''; < ''with''<sup>1</sup> + ''say''<sup>1</sup>.]   To speak against; contradict; deny; refuse.
{{smaller block|<poem>That i ''with-segge'',
Ne schal ihc hit biginne,
Til i suddene winne.</poem>
{{right|''King Horn'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 1276.}}}}

<poem>Finally, what wight that it ''withseyde'',
It was for nought.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, iv. 215.}}}}

{{smaller block|Of soch thynge herde I neuer speke, but by youre semblaunte ye seme alle worthi men, and therfore I will in no wise ''with-sey'' that ye requere, and be ye right welcome.
{{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), ii. 204.}}}}

'''withsayer†''' (wiᴛ̵ʜ-sā′ėr), ''n.''   [ME. ''withseier''; ''withsay'' + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.]   One who withsays; an opponent.

{{smaller block|That he be myȝti to much styre in holsum doctryne, and the ''withseieris'' to with stonde.
{{right|''Wyclif'', Pref. Ep., p. 63.}}}}

'''withset†''' (wiᴛ̵ʜ-set′), ''v. t.''   [< ME. ''withsetten'' (= G. ''widersetzen''); < ''with''<sup>1</sup> + ''set''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.'']   To set against; resist; oppose; withstand.

that cleerli schewith thee goostli liȝt

<poem>Of God the more grace thou hast serteyn,
If thou ''with-sett'' the devyl in his dede.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Coventry Mysteries'', p. 212.}}}}

'''with-sit†''', ''v. t.''   [ME. ''withsitten''; < ''with'' + ''sit''<sup>1</sup>.]   To oppose; contradict; withstand.

<poem>Was no beggere so bolde bote-yf he blynde were,
That dorst ''with-sitte'' that Peeres seyde for fere of syre
Hunger.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (C), ix. 202.}}}}

'''withstand''' (wiᴛ̵ʜ-stand′), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''withstood'', ppr. ''withstanding''.   [< ME. ''withstanden'', ''withstonden'' (pret. ''withstod'', pp. ''withstonde''), < AS. ''withstandan'' (pret. ''withstōd'', pp. ''withstanden'') (= Icel. ''vithstanda''; cf. G. ''widerstehen''), resist, withstand, < ''with'', against, + ''standan'', stand: see ''with''<sup>1</sup> and ''stand'', ''v.'']   '''I.''' ''trans.'' To stand against; oppose; resist, either with physical or with moral force: frequently with an implication of effectual resistance; resist or oppose successfully: as, to ''withstand'' the storm.

{{smaller block|{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, iv. 1298.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Wythstande'' the seruaunte that praysith the, for ellys he thynkyth the for to deceyve.
{{right|''Political Poems'', etc. (ed. Furnivall), p. 31.}}}}

{{smaller block|When Peter was come to Antioch, I ''withstood'' him to the face.
{{right|Gal. ii. 11.}}}}

{{smaller block|Youth and health have ''withstood'' well the involuntary and voluntary hardships of her lot.
{{right|''George Eliot'', Mill on the Floss, v. 1.}}}}

{{smaller block|<poem>Poor beauty! Time and fortune’s wrong
No shape nor feature may ''withstand;''
The wrecks are scattered all along,
Like emptied sea-shells on the sand.</poem>
{{right|''O. W. Holmes'', Mare Rubrum.}}}}
='''Syn.''' ''Resist'', etc. (see ''oppose''), confront, face.

{{smaller block|<poem>All affermyt hit fast with a fyn wyll,
Saue Ector the honerable, that egerly ''with-stod'',

“Hit is falshed in faythe & of fer cast!”</poem>
{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 7849.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>But Fate ''withstands'', and to oppose the attempt

{{right|''Milton'', P. L., ii. 610.}}}}

'''withstander''' (wiᴛʜ-stan′dėr), ''n.''   [< ''withstand'' + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.]   One who withstands; an opponent; a resisting power.

'''withwind''' (with′wīnd), ''n.''   [Also ''withywind;'' < ME. ''withwinde'', ''withewynde'', < AS. ''withewinde'', ''withwinde'' (= MD. ''wedewinde;'' cf. Icel. ''vithvindill'' = Dan. ''vedbende''), < ''withthe'', ''withig'', a flexible twig, + *''winde'', < ''windan'', wind: see ''withe'', ''withy'', and ''wind''<sup>1</sup>.]   The bindweed, ''Convolvulus''<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
